outputs.L1: We numerically investigate Barrett–Crane models of Riemannian quantum gravity. We extend existing numerical techniques to accommodate q-deformed models and arbitrary spacetime triangulations. For each model, we present and interpret expectation values for several selected observables, including a spin–spin correlation function that provides insight into the models’ behavior. We find the surprising result that, as the deformation parameter q approaches 1 through roots of unity, the limit is discontinuous.
outputs.L2: We carry out a numerical investigation of Barrett–Crane models for Riemannian quantum gravity. Existing computational methods are generalized so they can be applied both to q-deformed versions of the models and to general triangulations of spacetime. For each model, we report and analyze expectation values for several chosen observables, among them a spin–spin correlation function that sheds light on the models’ behavior. An unexpected outcome is that when the deformation parameter q approaches 1 along roots of unity, the limiting behavior is not continuous.

The study presents a numerical investigation of Barrett–Crane models in Riemannian quantum gravity. Its main goal is to explore the behavior of these spin foam models through computational methods, with particular attention to both the standard and q-deformed versions of the theory.

To carry out this analysis, the authors extend existing numerical techniques so that they can be applied more broadly. In particular, they adapt the methods to handle q-deformed Barrett–Crane models, where the deformation parameter q is typically taken to be a root of unity. They also generalize the approach so that it can be used for arbitrary space-time triangulations, rather than being restricted to special or highly symmetric cases. This makes the numerical framework more flexible and better suited to studying a wider class of quantum-gravity configurations.

The study then presents expectation values for a selection of observables in each of the models under consideration. These expectation values are interpreted in order to understand the physical and geometric content of the models, as well as how their behavior changes under q-deformation. By comparing the different cases, the authors are able to identify similarities and differences between the undeformed and deformed Barrett–Crane models.

A central diagnostic tool in the analysis is a spin–spin correlation function. This correlation function measures how spin variables associated with different parts of the triangulation are related to one another. By studying these correlations, the authors gain insight into the internal structure of the models and into the extent to which geometric degrees of freedom are correlated across the triangulated space-time.

One of the main conclusions of the study is that the limit in which the deformation parameter q approaches 1 is not continuous when q approaches 1 through roots of unity. In other words, the behavior of the q-deformed models does not smoothly reproduce the undeformed model in this limiting procedure. This discontinuity is an important result, as it suggests that q-deformation can have nontrivial effects on the numerical and physical properties of Barrett–Crane spin foam models, even in the regime where one might expect the undeformed theory to be recovered.

This study presents a numerical investigation of Barrett-Crane spin foam models of four-dimensional Riemannian quantum gravity. Building on earlier computational methods developed for the undeformed model, the work extends these techniques to the q-deformed case and to triangulations of arbitrary spacetime topology. In particular, the analysis considers models in which the deformation parameter q is taken to be a root of unity, a setting that provides a natural cutoff on the allowed representations and is often interpreted as introducing a nonzero cosmological constant.

The numerical framework is used to compute several observables associated with the spin foam amplitudes. Among these are spin expectation values and spin-spin correlation functions, which provide information about the distribution of geometric quantities and the way different parts of the triangulated spacetime are correlated. By evaluating these observables across different triangulations and for different values of the deformation parameter, the study explores how the q-deformed Barrett-Crane model behaves as the deformation is gradually removed.

A central focus of the work is the limit in which q approaches 1 through roots of unity. One might expect that, in this limit, the q-deformed model would smoothly reproduce the original undeformed Barrett-Crane model. However, the numerical results indicate that this expectation is not fulfilled. Instead, the study finds evidence that the q → 1 limit is discontinuous: the observables computed in the q-deformed models do not converge smoothly to the corresponding observables of the undeformed model.

This discontinuity is a surprising and significant result. It suggests that the q-deformed Barrett-Crane models are not merely regulated versions of the undeformed theory, at least not in a straightforward sense. The behavior of the model near q = 1 may therefore encode important structural differences between the deformed and undeformed formulations. These findings have implications for the interpretation of q-deformation in spin foam quantum gravity, the role of roots of unity as regulators, and the relationship between discrete quantum gravity models with and without a cosmological constant.

Overall, the study contributes both computational tools and new numerical evidence to the analysis of spin foam models. By extending simulations to q-deformed Barrett-Crane models on arbitrary triangulations and by examining observables such as spin-spin correlations, it provides a deeper understanding of the nonperturbative behavior of these models. The discovery of a discontinuous q → 1 limit highlights the need for further analytical and numerical work to clarify the continuum and semiclassical properties of spin foam approaches to quantum gravity.
outputs.L5:
The **Barrett–Crane model** is an important construction in the study of quantum gravity, particularly within the framework of spin foam models. It was proposed as a way to give a path-integral formulation of quantum gravity using ideas from topology, geometry, and representation theory.

In the **Riemannian** version of the Barrett–Crane model, spacetime is treated with a Euclidean rather than Lorentzian signature. This means the relevant symmetry group is associated with rotations in four-dimensional Euclidean space, typically involving groups such as \(SO(4)\) or its double cover \(Spin(4)\). The model assigns algebraic data to the elements of a triangulated four-dimensional manifold: faces, edges, and vertices receive labels related to group representations and intertwiners.

A central idea of the Barrett–Crane model is that four-dimensional geometry can be reconstructed from quantum data associated with simplices. In particular, the model uses “simple” representations, reflecting constraints that come from rewriting general relativity as a constrained topological field theory. These constraints are meant to reduce a topological BF theory to a theory with local gravitational degrees of freedom.

The Riemannian Barrett–Crane model played a major role in the development of spin foam quantum gravity. Although later models, such as the EPRL and FK models, refined or replaced some of its features, the Barrett–Crane construction remains historically and conceptually significant. It provided one of the first concrete proposals for describing quantum spacetime as a sum over discrete geometries, offering a bridge between loop quantum gravity, discrete geometry, and the path-integral approach to quantum gravity.

counterfactuals.output: We present numerical studies of q-deformed Barrett–Crane spin foam models for four-dimensional Riemannian quantum gravity with positive cosmological constant. Using finite state sums at roots of unity, we evaluate geometric observables associated with simplex volumes, face areas, and boundary spin configurations, with particular emphasis on spin–spin correlation functions as probes of semiclassical behavior. The q-deformation provides an infrared cutoff and renders the model finite, enabling systematic comparison across deformation parameters and boundary data. Our results show that correlations exhibit nontrivial dependence on q, boundary scale, and representation cutoff, with regimes suggestive of semiclassical geometric correlations but also significant deviations from the undeformed model. In particular, we identify a discontinuity in selected observables and spin–spin correlations in the limit q → 1, indicating that the undeformed Barrett–Crane model is not recovered smoothly from the q-deformed theory under the numerical limits considered. These findings highlight the subtle interplay between quantum group deformation, cosmological constant, and continuum-limit behavior in spin foam approaches to Riemannian quantum gravity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a research project extending numerical techniques for Barrett-Crane spin foam models to q-deformed cases and arbitrary spacetime triangulations.
counterfactuals.output:
The project extended existing numerical methods for evaluating Barrett–Crane spin foam models in two main directions: to **q-deformed models** and to **general spacetime triangulations**, rather than only highly symmetric or single-simplex cases.

Main findings:

- **Numerical evaluation of q-deformed Barrett–Crane amplitudes is feasible.**  
  The work showed that techniques previously used for the ordinary Barrett–Crane model can be adapted to the q-deformed case, where the deformation parameter \(q\) is related physically to a nonzero cosmological constant.

- **q-deformation improves finiteness properties.**  
  In the undeformed model, sums over spins can suffer from convergence issues. The q-deformed model naturally truncates or regulates the representation sums, making the state-sum amplitudes finite under suitable conditions.

- **Algorithms were generalized beyond a single 4-simplex.**  
  Earlier numerical studies often focused on isolated \(10j\)-symbols or very simple complexes. The project developed methods applicable to arbitrary triangulated spacetime regions, allowing full spin foam amplitudes to be computed for more general triangulations.

- **Efficient computation requires exploiting combinatorial structure.**  
  The amplitudes factor into local face, edge, and vertex contributions. By organizing the calculation around the triangulation’s incidence relations, the project made it possible to handle more complicated complexes systematically.

- **Asymptotic and numerical behavior can be studied in greater detail.**  
  The extended methods allow investigation of how amplitudes behave for large spin labels, how q-deformation changes this behavior, and whether semiclassical geometric features emerge.

- **The framework supports comparison between undeformed and q-deformed models.**  
  Because the numerical techniques apply to both cases, one can directly examine how introducing \(q\) changes amplitudes, convergence, and dependence on triangulation.

- **The work provides tools for testing spin foam quantum gravity beyond toy examples.**  
  By enabling computations on arbitrary triangulations, the project moves Barrett–Crane-type models closer to being numerically testable in realistic discrete spacetime settings.

In short, the project found that Barrett–Crane spin foam computations can be successfully extended to q-deformed models and to arbitrary triangulations, with q-deformation offering better control over divergences and the generalized algorithms making broader numerical exploration of spin foam quantum gravity possible.

counterfactuals.output:
**Title:** Numerical Expectation Values and the q-Deformation Limit in Barrett–Crane Quantum Gravity Models

We present a numerical study of spin-foam amplitudes in Barrett–Crane models of four-dimensional quantum gravity, with particular emphasis on the computation of expectation values for geometric observables and the behavior of the theory under q-deformation. Using Monte Carlo and direct summation techniques on finite triangulations, we evaluate amplitudes associated with areas, volumes, and correlation functions of boundary spin networks. These expectation values provide a probe of the semiclassical regime and of the extent to which discrete spin-foam configurations reproduce geometric behavior at large spins.

A central focus is the q-deformed Barrett–Crane model, where the deformation parameter introduces an effective cutoff in representation labels and is commonly associated with a nonzero cosmological constant. We investigate the approach to the undeformed limit as \(q \to 1\), analyzing convergence properties, cutoff dependence, and the stability of expectation values. Our simulations indicate that the q-deformation regularizes divergent contributions in a controlled manner, while the limiting behavior depends sensitively on the scaling of spin labels and triangulation size. In particular, we identify regimes in which geometric observables exhibit robust convergence, as well as regimes where residual cutoff effects remain significant.

These results clarify the numerical structure of Barrett–Crane spin foams and provide evidence for how q-deformation may serve as both a regulator and a physical modification of the model. The study also highlights practical challenges in extracting continuum and semiclassical physics from spin-foam state sums, including oscillatory amplitudes, large-spin asymptotics, and the interplay between boundary data and internal summations. Our findings contribute to ongoing efforts to test spin-foam quantum gravity models computationally and to understand the role of quantum-group deformation in defining finite, physically meaningful transition amplitudes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

Using finite triangulations of four-dimensional simplicial complexes, we evaluate spin foam amplitudes for both undeformed and \(q\)-deformed models, where the deformation provides a natural cutoff and is related to a nonzero cosmological constant. We analyze the convergence properties of the state sums, the scaling of amplitudes with refinement, and the sensitivity of observables to changes in triangulation. Boundary two-point correlation functions are computed for selected spin-network data, allowing a comparison between semiclassical expectations and the behavior of the discrete quantum amplitudes. Our results indicate that \(q\)-deformation improves numerical stability and suppresses large-spin contributions, while correlation functions display nontrivial dependence on both boundary geometry and the underlying triangulation. These findings provide quantitative evidence for the utility of quantum-group regularization in Barrett–Crane-type models and offer a basis for further numerical tests of four-dimensional spin foam dynamics.
